newsitem.title: UK: Leeson hid losses in secret account from start - FT.
newsitem.headline: Leeson hid losses in secret account from start - FT.

text.p: Nick Leeson, the Singapore trader who broke British merchant bank Barings last year, began hiding losses in a secret account within weeks of starting to trade in 1992, the Financial Times said on Wednesay.

Official inquiries into his affairs focused on 1994 when Leeson's losses grew rapidly. But the paper said he had sold derivatives to Barings customers at artifically low prices right from the start in an attempt to show his bosses he was a star.

"Leeson does not seem to have been motivated by personal gain, but was attempting to ensure a smooth start in his new job. However, the losses created to his improvements to futures prices later spiralled out of control," the paper said.

Leeson, now serving a six-and-a-half year jail term in Singapore, ran up almost $1.4 billion of losses in unauthorised derivatives trades. He used the secret accounts to hide his spiralling losses from bosses in London.

"By spring 1993, Leeson's execution of some kinds of futures trading was so far out of line with the rest of the market that Barings' customers were charged an extra commission for the opportunity to deal with him," the newspaper said.

Leeson himself said Barings sent money to Singapore for him because he convinced them he could make enormous profits. In fact, he was using the millions of pounds the London-based bank sent to cover his mounting losses.
"They were stupid, they were bumbling fools," Leeson told the BBC in June. "Every night I would ask for millions of pounds, and give them ridiculous stories -- and they would believe me."
In late July, German and British authorities dismissed a report claiming Leeson stashed 53 million marks ($35.53 million) in German bank accounts before Barings collapsed.
The bank was later rescued by Dutch financial giant Internationale Nederlanden Groep.
